sections.text: If, on the contrary, the sons of Dhritarashtra, with weapons in their hand, should slay me, unarmed and unresisting, surely that would be better for my welfare!
Sanjaya said: Having spoken thus, in the midst of the armies, Arjuna sank on the seat of the chariot, casting away his bow and arrow; heartbroken with grief.

We had been discussing Chapter 1, Arjuna Vishada Yoga, the Yoga of Arjunas Grief. We have come to the final concluding verses of Chapter 1. This chapter paints a scenario where thousands, if not millions, of people have gathered in Kurukshetra to do what they do best, to fight the war.
Kurukshetra is also called Dharmakshetra by Dhritarashtra in the first words. Dhritarashtra says, I want to know whats happening in Kurukshetra, which is a Dharmakshetra. Kurukshetra is analogous to Karmakshetra, the field of action. Its also called Dharmakshetra, which is analogous to a field of action where I can practice my Dharma, that which Im prepared for.
For an architect like me, Dharmakshetra is my office, where I practice the art of architecture. My Dharma as an architect is to design buildings. The field of action that gives me the opportunity to practice that art is my Dharmakshetra.
This scenario is analogous to the situations we find ourselves in our lives. Every year, universities have graduation ceremonies where we see a sea of students graduating, ready to enter the workforce. Obviously the question in the parents mind is: Will my son be successful in whatever profession he has prepared himself for? The thought comes to our mind that maybe the one with the most resources will be successful, a person who comes from a good family, has a family background, has a family business.
Or the other thought: maybe the one who is well-equipped, a good student with the highest grades, always ahead in class, that person will be the most successful. But experience in life shows us that both formulas do not work all the time. They may work sometimes, but not always.
What works all the time is character and integrity, that person will certainly be successful in life. Character-building is the goal of any scripture or study of scripture like Bhagavad Gita. The study of Bhagavad Gita has been called the Art of Man-Making. They were actually radio lectures by GM Bhagavad Gita, and he called them Art of Man Making.
So chapter one has prepared us to introspect and be aware of our own situations. So up till now, before we decided to learn Bhagavad Gita, we were facing the situation, but not very aware of what to look for, how to prepare ourselves for it. So therefore, this chapter is called Arjuna Vishadhi Yoga.
And theres always the question why this is the Yoga. Other chapters can be Yoga, but why this chapter is also called Yoga. This chapter actually united us with our own situations which we were oblivious about.
We did not know why I am doing what and why I am successful or I am failing. We are experiencing all these things, but we did not have a system to analyze and see what makes an activity successful or what makes my actions productive. So the study of Bhagavad Gita will now teach us, will prepare us to see situation comprehensively, and then we can decide how to act in this life.
And therefore its called Arjuna Vishadaya. It connected him to his own situation. So so far we have seen in this chapter that Arjun was very anxious while they were preparing for the war.
He considered himself to be something similar to a guy who has graduated at the top of his class and now hes entering workforce. He was always the best, and now he has this field of action where he can basically shine out. So typically we would have anticipated that he would be the last person to have any doubt about fighting this war.
They already debated whether this war is righteous or not. So before they gathered in the field of Kurukshetra, there were several incidents we see where Arjuna came out very confident. He told Sanjay, go tell Duryodhana that when Krishna and I are together, even Indras army cannot defeat us.
In the beginning of this Bisma Parva there are few _Verses_ where Judhisthe had doubt whether this war is right or not. And Arjuna was the one who gave him the right perspective and he gave him advice that there will be time where fighting war is the only right thing to do for the righteous cause. He said, as long as our cause, they are righteous, we will be the winners.
So hes pretty confident. He was in control of his own situation. And then suddenly when he saw all the relatives on both sides, he somehow had nervous breakdown.
He had a completely different perception of whats happening. All hes confident about fighting this war not because we want this kingdom, but its the right thing to do. The cause is right, therefore we have to fight this war.
The only thing he saw at that point, I have to kill my own cousins and my own teacher and my own grandfather. So he was more overruled by the attachment than the principal. So then we have seen that he had a nervous breakdown, his anxiety, and then he basically has delusion.
When he had delusion, he started seeing reality completely differently. Therefore he started making argument about why he does not want to fight this war. So his first argument was, well, they are not smart enough to figure out that this is not a right thing to do, but we are better than them.
He put himself on a pedestal saying, I am better than them. They dont know what they are doing, but we know, and therefore we shouldnt be fighting this war. When that argument did not work with Krishna, because he was obviously looking for validation from Krishna that yes, hes on the right path, well, we always try to avoid this war.
Arjuna, Im glad that you realize at the end its not too late. Lets pack our bags and go home. In verse 37 he has already declared that he said, therefore, lets not participate in this war.
We have not heard from Krishna yet. So now he makes a greater moral argument why the war itself is sinful. War in any shape and form is sinful.
He is the first conscientious objector in the history promoting the pacifist argument about why war should not be fought. Buddha was pacifist, obviously. He promoted that war should not be fought.
That was a very different outlook all his life. Right from the beginning. Buddha saw the thing very differently.
The Vedantic tradition does not see it that way. Suddenly he became pacifist when people were relying on him to fight this battle. So now he makes a moral argument saying that war is sinful because it destroys the family unit.
Family unit, which is the basic unit for the society, as we discussed last time, that at that time and even till today, family is the unit which makes any society the families are educated, the society will be educated. So whatever is happening at the microcosm in a family will be happening in the macrocosm in the society. So therefore, protecting families is very important, very valid argument he makes then.
We have seen that as we progressed in the modern time, the family unit became a couple and the couple became an individual. So now we have individual right is what we are trying to protect. So he makes argument to Krishna that by fighting this war, well be destroying families, and therefore we will be the sinners.
Because we will be the cause for destroying this family unit, which will ultimately will destroy the entire culture in the society. In a family, the man has the duty to protect and provide for the family. So theres a division of labor.
Man is providing and protecting the family, woman is nurturing the family. And in that situation, if you take the protector and provider away, the nurturer has no resources to nurture the family. And therefore the nurturer will become corrupt, corruption.
She has to do something which is not appropriate for her to get out of her role of nurturer into a provider. And that will eventually make the nurturing part of the family suffer. If family is not nurtured, the next generation, the society will suffer.
We hear in our society that the children who grow up without any family, they obviously will not have the right values. They do not know what is the right of their life. We have Hindi movies where this hero becomes a gangster because he grew up on the streets and he did not have any support, any guidance from the family.
So its a valid argument he makes that we cannot disrupt this family unit. And therefore he said that we will be the sinner and the one who destroys the family unit. That person will go to hell forever.
In other words, we will be the cause for creating hell in this society. So it continues argument and says. He makes a moral argument about our responsibility to preserve our culture and social structure.
Once we destroy the family, we have destroyed that order. And therefore those men who participate in that, they will go to hell forever. Utsun kuladharmana Manushyana Janardhana Narake Niyatam Vasaha Bhavati anushushrama.
Those men, as you say, will go to hell forever. Traditionally, if you just believe in that, after your death you will be either go to swarga or Narak. Then see in this case, because you definitely going to hell.
But the broader view of that is that the society will live in hell and you will be part of it. You will be living in hell. If the law and order in this society is destroyed by whatever is happening because the corruption people start behaving as if they have all the rights then the overall atmosphere in the society will become not livable every more hellish living.
Ahobat Mahatpapam kartum Vyavasita Vayam. You know, basically has concluded his argument and said Ahubat alas Mahat papam kartam Vavasitavayam. He actually tells conclusively to Krishna we engage in this great sin by fighting this war, destroying this family and culture and society.
We are sending everyone to hell. Hellish living for everyone. And that is only for Yad Rajya Sukh Lovina.
We are only doing it because we want this kingdom. Our greed to have this kingdom is motivating us to engage in this act which is sinful. Yadi Maam pratikaram Asastram Sastra Panayah Dartarashtra Rane Hanyuhu Tanme Shemataram Bhaved.
Therefore he is my final decision that even the Dhritarashtras sons kill me with their weapons and me having no weapons in my hand that will be better for me than killing my own kids and kids. You know, he came to the conclusion that in this life if I can think of what will give me the liberation from my situation that is a better liberation than me fighting the war and winning what is rightfully mine. He makes a much greater argument to preserve rightfully theirs with the Kshema.
Yoga is something we are trying to achieve which we dont have. Shema is something we have and we are trying to protect it like Shema. So you see, the first argument for fighting this war is for the Shema.

Verse 46 contains Arjunas final, dramatic declaration: Yadi mam apratikaram ashastram shastra-panayah dhartarashtrah rane hanyuh tan me kshemataram bhavet, If Dhritarashtras sons, weapons in hand, were to kill me unarmed and unresisting on the battlefield, that would be BETTER for my welfare (kshemataram). This is complete psychological collapse, the greatest warrior in the world declaring that being killed defenseless would be preferable to fighting. Then verse 47, the chapters conclusion: Evam uktva arjunah sankhye rathopastha upavishat, visrijya sa-sharam chapam shoka-samvigna-manasah, Having spoken thus, Arjuna sat down on the seat of his chariot in the midst of battle, casting aside his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed with grief (shoka). The image is complete: the hero who commanded Krishna confidently now sits collapsed, weapon abandoned, heart broken. This is why the chapter is called Arjuna Vishada Yoga, the Yoga of Arjunas Despair. Yoga means union, connection. Through his grief, Arjuna has finally connected with the true complexity of his situation. His previous confidence was based on incomplete seeing. Now, overwhelmed, he is finally ready to learn. The Gita teaches that wisdom often begins in crisis, that the shattering of false certainty creates space for true understanding. Calls this the Art of Man-Making, character is built not in ease but in struggle. Reflect on your own verse 47 moments, times when youve sat down in the midst of battle, dropped your weapons, overwhelmed. These moments, painful as they are, may be exactly when you become ready for deeper teaching. What wisdom might be waiting for you on the other side of your current despair?
